title: Choose the Tutor workspace
question: Which structure should make Tutor feel most useful for explanations, decisions, and consented study actions?

options.label: Situation Desk
options.thesis: Tutor turns each question into a concise academic brief: what matters, what it checked, and what it can do next. A narrow action docket stays visible beside the answer until the student approves or dismisses each proposal.
options.materials: Warm paper workspace, one navy briefing plane, white conversation sheet, full-span rules, indigo for scope and consent only.
options.risk: The action docket must remain contextual or it will become a second dashboard competing with the conversation.

options.label: Tutor Workbench
options.thesis: A calm, document-like conversation fills the page. Scope, sources, remembered plans, and proposed actions open as full-width ruled drawers beneath the relevant answer, keeping reading central and evidence close to the claim.
options.materials: Editorial answer sheet, flush disclosure rows, quiet scope chips, no permanent inner rail, dark composer only at the point of action.
options.risk: Without a persistent action region, multi-step plans could be easier to overlook after a long explanation.

options.label: Study Brief
options.thesis: Tutor opens on a compact briefing of today’s risks, plans, and course signals, then continues as a workspace-wide dialogue. The current course or lecture appears as an explicit lens that the student can widen at any time.
options.materials: Departure-board hierarchy, restrained signal tint, ruled briefing rows, one anchored composer, compact evidence drawer.
options.risk: The opening brief may feel like another Home page unless it quickly yields to the active conversation.
